words.definition: A reflexive jolt when something changes without warning. The body responds before the mind has decided whether the interruption is dangerous, welcome, or harmless.
words.labelingNote: If this word fits, the naming has already started to work: labeling an emotion precisely measurably lowers its intensity.

nearby.contrast: Wonder that changes your sense of scale. Startled centers on the body reacting before meaning is clear.
A reality that sharply violates expectation. Startled centers on the body reacting before meaning is clear.

techniques.name: Orient to the present
techniques.body: Put both feet down and name three facts that are true now. Startled centers on the body reacting before meaning is clear; present facts give the nervous system a stable frame before interpretation takes over.
techniques.whereItBreaks: facts do not settle a body that is still in danger. Move to safety first, then orient.

techniques.name: Name what changed
techniques.body: Complete two lines: “I expected ___” and “instead ___.” The gap shows exactly what startled is asking your mind to update.
techniques.whereItBreaks: forcing an explanation too quickly replaces uncertainty with a convenient story. Leave the blank open when you do not know.

techniques.name: Choose one question
techniques.body: Ask the smallest question that would make the situation more legible, then seek only that answer. One good question turns surprise into information without demanding total certainty.
techniques.whereItBreaks: some events need time, not investigation. If more information is flooding you, pause the search.

words.definition: High-energy anticipation of something wanted or newly possible. The body mobilizes toward the future, making attention quick, expansive, and ready to act.

techniques.name: Stay with the signal
techniques.body: Notice how excited feels in the body for twenty uninterrupted seconds before reaching for a screen, explanation, or next task. Attention helps a positive state register instead of passing unnoticed.
techniques.whereItBreaks: trying to hold the feeling can turn savoring into pressure. Let it change when it changes.

techniques.name: Name the source
techniques.body: Finish the sentence “This feeling came from ___.” Be specific about the person, effort, condition, or moment so you can recognize what supports it.
techniques.whereItBreaks: do not turn good fortune into a demand to optimize every future moment. Recognition is enough.

techniques.name: Let it move
techniques.body: Choose one proportionate expression: tell someone, mark the moment, offer thanks, or repeat the nourishing condition. Positive emotion becomes more usable when it has a clean outlet.
techniques.whereItBreaks: sharing can become performance if you need a particular reaction. Choose an expression that remains worthwhile on its own.

words.definition: A bittersweet pull toward a past that felt meaningful, safe, or alive. Nostalgia revisits what is gone while preserving the warmth of having had it.
words.labelingNote: If this word fits, the naming has already started to work: labeling an emotion precisely measurably lowers its intensity.

nearby.contrast: A judgment that condemns the whole self. Nostalgic centers on longing that keeps the warmth of a meaningful past.

techniques.name: Make room for the feeling
techniques.body: Set a short, protected interval to notice nostalgic without arguing with it. Locate it in the body and let the feeling be information rather than a verdict.
techniques.whereItBreaks: unstructured immersion can deepen a spiral. Use a time boundary and return to food, sleep, movement, or company.

techniques.name: Name what is missing
techniques.body: Complete “I feel nostalgic because I wanted or valued ___.” Nostalgic centers on longing that keeps the warmth of a meaningful past; naming the missing thing clarifies whether it can be repaired, sought, or mourned.
techniques.whereItBreaks: not every loss contains a lesson or action. Do not manufacture one to avoid grief.

techniques.name: Choose contact or care
techniques.body: Ask whether this moment needs witness, practical help, repair, or gentle routine. Make one small request or act of care that matches the answer.
techniques.whereItBreaks: the wrong audience can increase exposure or shame. Choose someone able to respond, or begin with private care.

words.definition: The mind and body adapting to a loss that cannot simply be reversed. Grief reaches beyond sadness: it reorganizes habits, identity, expectation, and the shape of daily life.

techniques.name: Make room for the feeling
techniques.body: Set a short, protected interval to notice grieving without arguing with it. Locate it in the body and let the feeling be information rather than a verdict.
techniques.whereItBreaks: unstructured immersion can deepen a spiral. Use a time boundary and return to food, sleep, movement, or company.

techniques.name: Name what is missing
techniques.body: Complete “I feel grieving because I wanted or valued ___.” Grieving centers on the whole-person adjustment to irreversible loss; naming the missing thing clarifies whether it can be repaired, sought, or mourned.
techniques.whereItBreaks: not every loss contains a lesson or action. Do not manufacture one to avoid grief.

techniques.name: Choose contact or care
techniques.body: Ask whether this moment needs witness, practical help, repair, or gentle routine. Make one small request or act of care that matches the answer.
techniques.whereItBreaks: the wrong audience can increase exposure or shame. Choose someone able to respond, or begin with private care.

techniques.name: Create clean distance
techniques.body: Reduce contact long enough to let the first wave of the feeling settle: step back, close the tab, ventilate, or pause the conversation. Distance makes choice possible when you feel alienated.

techniques.name: Locate the boundary
techniques.body: Finish “This feels unacceptable because ___.” Alienated centers on estrangement from a place of expected belonging; identify the concrete behavior, substance, or value violation rather than condemning a whole person.
techniques.whereItBreaks: a boundary stated as a character judgment invites contempt instead of useful protection. Keep it behavioral.

techniques.name: Check the verdict
techniques.body: Separate what you directly observed from what you inferred about contamination, intent, or worth. Keep the protective signal while testing the conclusion it produced.
techniques.whereItBreaks: analysis is not required when the evidence already shows a real safety or consent violation. Act on the boundary.

words.definition: Anger that has settled in around a specific unfairness — usually one you keep re-encountering, and often aimed at someone you haven't confronted. It accumulates: each new instance lands on the pile of the old ones.
words.labelingNote: If this word fits, the naming has already started to work: labeling an emotion precisely measurably lowers its intensity.

nearby.contrast: resentment that has stopped expecting repair. Resentment still holds a live claim; bitterness has filed it away as how things are.
hotter and more public. Indignation is anger at unfairness on principle, often on someone else's behalf; resentment keeps a personal ledger.

techniques.name: Name the cost
techniques.body: Write the sentence “I'm resentful because X keeps costing me Y.” Be exact about X and Y. Precision turns a mood into a claim you can check against the facts.
techniques.whereItBreaks: if the sentence stops changing from day to day, writing has become rehearsal. Stop refining the grievance and act on it.

techniques.name: Reappraise the story
techniques.body: Look for the least-damning explanation that still fits every fact — “they're overloaded,” not “they don't respect me.” If it genuinely fits, the resentment loses its target.
techniques.whereItBreaks: misused, reappraisal rationalizes an arrangement you should renegotiate or leave. If the facts really are unfair, no better story fixes that.

techniques.name: Make the request
techniques.body: Resentment usually marks an unspoken contract someone keeps breaking. Say the term out loud to the person who can change it: one sentence, no case file.
techniques.whereItBreaks: only works where someone can actually grant it. If you've asked twice and nothing moved, the next step is a consequence, not a third ask.

words.definition: Very high-intensity anger that mobilizes the body for immediate action. Fury narrows attention around the offense and can make force feel necessary before judgment has caught up.
words.labelingNote: If this word fits, the naming has already started to work: labeling an emotion precisely measurably lowers its intensity.

nearby.contrast: Small recurring friction that keeps catching attention. Furious centers on anger intense enough to demand immediate action.
Anger that places its target below respect. Furious centers on anger intense enough to demand immediate action.

techniques.name: Lower the heat before acting
techniques.body: Delay the message or decision until your body is below the peak of the feeling. Use brisk movement, slower exhalations, or cold water, then return to what made you furious.
techniques.whereItBreaks: calming down must not become abandoning a legitimate claim. Set a time to return to it.

techniques.name: Name the blocked value
techniques.body: Complete “I am furious because ___ is blocking or violating ___.” Furious centers on anger intense enough to demand immediate action; precision separates the value from the first impulse.
techniques.whereItBreaks: a value is not proof that your preferred remedy is fair. Check impact and constraints before acting.

techniques.name: Make one clean move
techniques.body: Choose the smallest action that protects the value: a request, boundary, consequence, repair, or exit. State it without a case file or attack on character.
techniques.whereItBreaks: some situations are unsafe or structurally fixed. When direct action carries real risk, seek support and plan before confronting.

distinctions.guilty|ashamed: Guilt is about what you did; shame is about what you are. Guilt points at an act you could repair. Shame points at the self — which is why it makes you hide.
distinctions.envious|jealous: Envy wants something someone else has. Jealousy guards something you already have against losing it to someone else.
distinctions.anxious|worried: Worry loops on a specific problem and stays mostly in words. Anxiety is the body bracing for a threat that may have no name yet.
distinctions.disappointed|discouraged: Disappointment is about an outcome that fell short. Discouragement is about whether to keep trying at all.
distinctions.nostalgic|grieving: Both look back. Nostalgia visits a past that felt good, and returns. Grief reaches for something that is not coming back.
distinctions.bitter|resentful: Resentment still holds a live claim against someone. Bitterness has stopped expecting repair and settled into how things are.

adoptedSeeds.definition: Longing for someone or something loved and absent, knowing it may not return.
